title: Met, Found Out, Refused: Verbs That Change Meaning

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know from B2 Unit 2 that *conocer*, *saber*, *querer* and *poder* change meaning in the past. In the imperfect they name a state (I knew, I wanted, I was able); in the preterite they name an event with a start or an end, and the meaning shifts: I met, I found out, I tried or refused, I managed. Stories of songs and films are full of such moments.

sections.title: Same verb, two tenses
rows: Conocía el son. / Conocí a un trovador.
I knew the son. / I met a troubadour (for the first time).
Sabía la letra. / Supe la noticia ayer.
I knew the lyrics. / I found out the news yesterday.
He wanted to leave. / He refused to leave.
He was able to sing. / He managed to sing.

items.spanish: Sergio no quiso irse de Cuba con su familia.
items.english: Sergio refused to leave Cuba with his family.

items.spanish: El gobierno quiso crear un cine propio y fundó el ICAIC en 1959.
items.english: The government set out to create its own cinema and founded the ICAIC in 1959.

items.spanish: Ayer conocí a un trovador cubano en un concierto.
items.english: Yesterday I met a Cuban troubadour at a concert.

items.spanish: Cuando conocí el son, no sabía que había nacido en el este de la isla.
items.english: When I got to know the son, I did not know it had been born in the east of the island.

sections.content: Do not translate by tense alone: ask whether something happened (an event) or how things were (a state). In the negative, *no quiso* is a refusal, *no pudo* means you tried and did not manage, and *no quería* and *no podía* only say how things stood.
